data.text: @0xChaseTM the "my job is to write loops" line is the whole shift, and you framed it perfectly. saving this one

Prompt engineering is dead.

We're entering the era of "loop engineering" - where your agents prompt themselves to complete tasks.

Lance Martin ( @RLanceMartin ) from Anthropic just leaked the entire playbook for using loops in Claude properly.

How to run loops with Claude models (step-by-step)

First - understand what a loop actually is.

Instead of prompting Claude manually, you design a system where Claude runs, collects feedback, self-corrects, and keeps going until the goal is met.

The head of Claude Code (Boris) said it best:

"My job is to write loops."

Step 1. Define a goal or rubric

Give Claude a clear rubric with checkable criteria.

Example: "Run a baseline, run 20 experiments, document each result, improve on the last."

Use /goal in Claude Code or Outcomes in Claude Managed Agents; these are the built-in primitives for applying this.

Step 2. Add a verifier sub-agent

Don't let Claude grade its own work.

Instead, launch a verifier sub-agent that grades the outputs.

Outcomes in Claude Managed Agents handle this automatically.

Step 3. Build a memory system

Opus is most powerful when it has a memory log, allowing it to self-evolve over time.

Fail → Investigate → Verify → Distill → Consult

Claude then writes lessons to memory during a session, and in future sessions, retrieves and applies them.

Step 4. Let it run

Once you set you /loop prompt. Just let it run until the deliverables are met.

I personally like this prompting structure: /loop + <time interval> + <goal>

This is the most powerful way to run Claude models right now.

999 will quietly bleed your account dry. Every single one of them looks like a winner.

One method pulls the real one out. Quant desks have run it for years. It's called loop engineering.

It's not a smarter prompt. It's a loop: generate a strategy, test it, score why it failed, feed that back, and run it again until one survives data it has never seen.

Man Group runs $150 billion. They built an AI that writes and tests hundreds of strategies a week.

And second agent whose only job is to hunt the ones that secretly overfit and kill them before a cent goes live. 

> describe an idea -> backtest 5 years in 12 seconds
> read why it died -> feed that back in
> run it again until one survives data it never saw

AI can write a thousand strategies. Loop engineering is the only thing that tells you which one was ever real.

89% of retail lost money in 2025. Almost none of it from bad ideas. All of it from trading the first guess and never running it through backtest loop.

Alpha research is just a pipeline. So instead of sitting in it, you hand each stage to its own agent:

> one reads every new research paper overnight and pulls out the trade idea
> one builds the features and cleans the data
> one backtests it over 20 years, costs and slippage included
> one runs the hard stats and kills anything overfit
> one checks it still works in every market regime
> one strips out plain momentum and value to see if any real edge is left

Each of those six is a job a fund pays a $600,000-a-year quant to do. 

He runs all six for the price of an API bill.

The rule that makes it work: the agent that builds a signal never gets to approve it. 

A separate, stronger agent tries to kill it first. Whatever survives all six by morning is real, new alpha.
